title: Sample 13-9: Lines of Poetry with Stress Marks

illustrates.quote: Transcribe a poem that contains stress, scansion, or meter marks twice. Place the two versions on a single braille page if possible. The first version should include the title and author or other attribution.

blocks.features: Two-line e.e. cummings excerpt ('seen from above, the sky / is deep. clouds float down there,'), shown twice in print: first with breve/acute stress marks placed above individual syllables, then repeated as a diagram of stress marks with the words replaced by underscores/spacing beneath a second, differently-capitalised rendering.

lines.text: Is deep. Clouds float down there,

print.notes: Picture on PDF p.377; only the two-line excerpt and its stress-mark diagram are shown (a genuine excerpt: printed line numbers begin at 4), matching the 'Sample:' note under rule 13.9.3.g which explains this twice-shown technique.
print.printFeatures: Breve (˘) and acute (′)-style stress marks placed above syllables in each rendering.

braille.notes: Verbatim from .txt lines 10886-10902 (excerpt; printed line numbers begin at 4), after stripping a 5-char line-number field (2-digit max line number 20, +3=5) and converting U+2800. Lines 1-5 are the transcriber's note (identical wording to rule 13.9.3.g's own 'Sample:' text) plus its 2-row symbols key, inside a grade-1 passage. Lines 10-11 are the FIRST writing (contracted braille, no stress marks). Lines 13-14 and 16-17 are the SECOND writing (uncontracted, cell-3 offset per rule 13.9.3.c), each poetic line preceded by its own stress-symbol row directly above it, per rule 13.9.3.e.
